steps.body: Sign + 4 digits $=5$ characters $=5$ bytes.

steps.title: Integer form
steps.body: $|v|\le 9999<2^{15}=32768$, so a 16-bit (2-byte) signed integer suffices.

optionAnalysis.reason: 80% would mean only 1 byte for the integer, which cannot hold ±9999.
20% would mean a 4-byte integer.
Correct: 5 bytes → 2 bytes.
40% would mean a 3-byte integer — not a standard width and more than needed.

pitfalls: Forgetting the sign character (would give $4\to2$, i.e. 50%).
cse-1998-a-55.verification: $2/5=40\%$ of the original remains, i.e. 60% saved.

cse-1998-a-56-a.approach: Model arrival times $X,Y$ as independent uniform on $[0,60]$ minutes. They meet iff $|X-Y|\le10$ (the end-of-hour cap never cuts a wait short of the other's arrival, since both arrive by 60). Compute the complementary area.

steps.title: Meeting condition
steps.body: If $X\le Y$, the first friend waits until $\min(X+10,60)$; since $Y\le60$, they meet iff $Y-X\le10$. Symmetrically, meet $\iff |X-Y|\le10$.

steps.title: Non-meeting region
steps.body:
In the $60\times60$ square, $|X-Y|>10$ is two right triangles with legs $50$:

$$2\times\tfrac12\times50\times50=2500$$

steps.title: Probability
steps.body: $P(\text{not meet})=\dfrac{2500}{3600}=\dfrac{25}{36}\approx0.694$.

pitfalls: Reporting $11/36$, the probability that they do meet.

cse-1998-a-56-b.approach: Each 0 needs at least $k$ 1s immediately before it and exactly $k$ 1s immediately after it. So the first 0 is preceded by $1^k1^*$, consecutive 0s are separated by exactly $1^k$ (which also supplies the "at least $k$" for the next 0), and the string ends with $1^k$ after the last 0.

steps.title: Strings without 0
steps.body: No 0 means no constraint: $1^*$.

steps.title: Strings with 0s
steps.body: Before the first 0: $1^k1^*$ (at least $k$ ones). Every 0 is followed by exactly $1^k$, then either the end or another 0. That $1^k$ block also gives the next 0 its $k$ preceding ones. So the tail is $(01^k)^+$.

pitfalls: Allowing $1^*$ after the last $01^k$, which would let a 0 be followed by more than $k$ ones.
cse-1998-a-56-b.verification: $k=2$: $11011011$ is accepted ($11\cdot011\cdot011$); $1011$ (only one 1 before the 0) and $110111$ (three 1s after) are rejected.

cse-1998-a-57.approach: Track the value mod 5 while reading bits MSB first: appending bit $b$ maps remainder $r$ to $(2r+b)\bmod5$. Leading zeros keep remainder 0, so they are ignored automatically. The 5 remainders are pairwise distinguishable, so 5 states are minimum.

steps.title: Transition rule
steps.body: If the prefix read so far has value $v\equiv r\pmod5$, after bit $b$ the value is $2v+b\equiv 2r+b\pmod 5$. States $q_0..q_4$ = remainder; start = accept = $q_0$.

steps.title: Trace 1010 (= 10)
steps.body: $q_0\xrightarrow{1}q_1\xrightarrow{0}q_2\xrightarrow{1}q_0\xrightarrow{0}q_0$ — accepted, and indeed $10=2\times5$.

steps.title: Minimality
steps.body: For remainders $r\ne s$ the states are distinguishable: pick a suffix $w$ taking $r$ to 0; it takes $s$ to a different remainder since $x\mapsto 2^{|w|}x+c$ is a bijection mod 5. Hence 5 states is the minimum.

answer.value: 5-state DFA with states = remainder mod 5; δ(r, b) = (2r + b) mod 5; start and only final state = 0

pitfalls: Adding a separate state for leading zeros — unnecessary, since $0$ keeps $q_0$ on $q_0$.

cse-1998-a-57-a.approach: IMP computes $a\to b=\overline a+b$. Write $f=x\overline y+\overline x y$ in the form $\overline a+b$: $f=g_1\to\overline{g_2}$ with $g_1=x\to y$ and $g_2=y\to x$; the negation $\overline{g_2}=g_2\to0$ needs the constant 0.

steps.title: Gate identities
steps.body: $a\to b=\overline a+b$, so $a\to0=\overline a$ and $\overline{x\to y}=x\overline y$.

steps.title: Construction
steps.body:
$g_1=x\to y=\overline x+y$

$g_2=y\to x=\overline y+x$

$g_3=g_2\to0=\overline{g_2}=\overline x\,y$

$f=g_1\to g_3=\overline{g_1}+g_3=x\overline y+\overline x y$ ✓ (4 gates)

steps.title: Why the constant 0 is needed
steps.body: IMP is 1-preserving: $1\to1=1$. Any circuit of IMP gates fed only by $x,y$ outputs 1 when $x=y=1$, but $f(1,1)=0$. So a constant-0 input is unavoidable.

cse-1998-a-57-a.verification: Truth table: $(x,y)=(0,0)$: $g_1=1,g_3=0\Rightarrow f=0$; $(0,1)$: $g_3=1\Rightarrow f=1$; $(1,0)$: $g_1=0\Rightarrow f=1$; $(1,1)$: $g_1=1,g_3=0\Rightarrow f=0$ ✓.

cse-1998-a-57-b.approach: Build a known complete set: NOT from $x\to0$ and OR from $(x\to0)\to y$. Since {NOT, OR} is functionally complete, so is IMP (with the constant 0).

steps.title: NOT gate
steps.body: $x\to0=\overline x+0=\overline x$.

steps.title: OR gate
steps.body: $(x\to0)\to y=\overline{\overline x}+y=x+y$.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: {NOT, OR} is complete (AND by De Morgan: $xy=\overline{\overline x+\overline y}$), hence every Boolean function can be built from IMP gates and the constant 0.

answer.value: x→0 = x̄ (NOT); (x→0)→y = x + y (OR); {NOT, OR} is complete

pitfalls: Claiming completeness without a constant: IMP alone preserves 1, so the constant 0 is required.
cse-1998-a-57-b.verification: AND directly: $(x\to(y\to0))\to0=\overline{\overline x+\overline y}=xy$; truth table confirms all four rows.

cse-1998-a-58-a.approach: Shift away the constant: the fixed point of $x = 2x - 1$ is $x = 1$, so $y_n = x_n - 1$ satisfies a pure doubling recurrence.
pitfalls: Writing $2^n + 1$ — that gives $x_1 = 3$, not 2.

cse-1998-a-58-b.approach: The recursion is indirect ($S \Rightarrow Aa$, $A \Rightarrow Sd$), so first substitute $S$ into the $A$-rule to expose immediate left recursion, then apply the standard $A \to A\alpha \mid \beta$ rewrite.

steps.title: Expose the recursion
steps.body:
Replace $S$ in $A \to Sd$ by its alternatives $Aa \mid b$:
$$A \to Ac \mid Aad \mid bd \mid \epsilon$$
Now every left recursion is immediate: $\alpha_1 = c,\ \alpha_2 = ad$; non-recursive $\beta_1 = bd,\ \beta_2 = \epsilon$.

steps.title: Apply the $A \to \beta A'$ rewrite
steps.body:
For $A \to A\alpha_1 \mid A\alpha_2 \mid \beta_1 \mid \beta_2$:
$$A \to bdA' \mid A'\qquad A' \to cA' \mid adA' \mid \epsilon$$
($\beta_2 = \epsilon$ gives $A \to A'$.)

steps.title: Final grammar
steps.body:
$$S \to Aa \mid b$$
$$A \to bdA' \mid A'$$
$$A' \to cA' \mid adA' \mid \epsilon$$
Both describe $A = (bd \mid \epsilon)(c \mid ad)^*$, so the language is unchanged, and no non-terminal derives itself as a leftmost symbol.

answer.value: $S \to Aa \mid b;\ A \to bdA' \mid A';\ A' \to cA' \mid adA' \mid \epsilon$

pitfalls: Only removing $A \to Ac$ and leaving $A \to Sd$: $A \Rightarrow Sd \Rightarrow Aad$ is still left recursive.
Forgetting the $\epsilon$ alternative of $A$, which becomes $A \to A'$.
cse-1998-a-58-b.verification: Both grammars give $A = (bd\mid\epsilon)(c\mid ad)^*$ and $S = Aa \mid b$.

cse-1998-a-59-a.approach: Join the three relations so that the parlor matches (FREQUENTS–SERVES) and both the student and the ice-cream match (SERVES–LIKES, FREQUENTS–LIKES); project the student with DISTINCT.

steps.title: Condition to express
steps.body: Student $s$ qualifies if there exist $p, i$ with $(s,p) \in$ FREQUENTS, $(p,i) \in$ SERVES and $(s,i) \in$ LIKES.

steps.title: SQL
steps.body:
Hyphenated names are written with underscores (or quoted):
```sql
SELECT DISTINCT F.student
FROM   FREQUENTS F, SERVES S, LIKES L
WHERE  F.parlor     = S.parlor
  AND  S.ice_cream  = L.ice_cream
  AND  F.student    = L.student;
```

steps.title: Why DISTINCT
steps.body: A student may match through several parlors or ice-creams; DISTINCT prints each student once. An equivalent form uses `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM SERVES S, LIKES L WHERE ...)`.

answer.value: SELECT DISTINCT F.student FROM FREQUENTS F, SERVES S, LIKES L WHERE F.parlor = S.parlor AND S.ice_cream = L.ice_cream AND F.student = L.student

pitfalls: Dropping $F.student = L.student$ — that would list students whose parlor serves an ice-cream liked by *someone*.
cse-1998-a-59-a.verification: Each WHERE conjunct corresponds to one membership in the existential condition of step 1.

cse-1998-a-59-b.approach: Simulate the fixed partitions over time: at each instant, take waiting jobs in arrival order and give each the smallest free partition that fits (best fit). The 20K job can only use the 20K partition, so just track that partition.

steps.title: At t = 0
steps.body: J1 (2K) → P4 (2K), runs 0–4. J2 (14K) → P3 (20K, the only one ≥ 14K), runs 0–10. J3 (3K) → P1 (4K), runs 0–2. J4 (6K) → P2 (8K), runs 0–1. J5 waits.

scene.caption: t = 0: J1, J2, J3, J4 placed by best fit

steps.title: Small jobs in P1, P2
steps.body: t = 1: P2 frees → J5 (6K) → P2, runs 1–5. t = 2: P1 (4K) frees, but the next job J6 (10K) needs ≥ 10K — only P3 qualifies.

scene.caption: J5 takes P2 at t = 1; J6 must wait for P3

steps.title: The 20K partition
steps.body: P3 is busy with J2 until $t = 10$. Then J6 (10K) runs $10 \to 10 + 1 = 11$, and J7 (20K) gets P3 at 11 and runs $11 \to 11 + 8 = 19$.

steps.title: Where J8 goes does not matter
steps.body: J8 (2K) never needs P3 (it best-fits into P4 or P1). Whether it runs early (P1 at t = 2) or after J7 is placed (P4 at 11–17), the 20K job still completes at **19**.

pitfalls: Treating memory as variable partitions (holes merge) — here the partitions are fixed.
Letting the 10K job use the 8K partition.
cse-1998-a-59-b.verification: Both 10K and 20K jobs fit only in P3, so the completion of J7 is $10 + 1 + 8 = 19$ regardless of the other jobs.

cse-1998-b-60-a.approach: Set $f'(x) = 0$, then classify each critical point with the sign of $f''$.

steps.title: Endpoints for context
steps.body: $f(0) = 15$, $f(6) = 216 - 216 + 54 + 15 = 69$. So on $[0,6]$ the global maximum is 69 at $x = 6$; the interior local extrema are at $x = 1$ and $x = 3$.

answer.value: Local maximum at $x = 1$ ($f = 19$), local minimum at $x = 3$ ($f = 15$)

pitfalls: Reading the printed $-6x + 9x$ literally gives $x^3 + 3x + 15$, which is increasing and has no extrema — the square was lost in printing.
cse-1998-b-60-a.verification: Sign of $f'$: positive on $(0,1)$, negative on $(1,3)$, positive on $(3,6)$ — max then min.

cse-1998-b-60-b.approach: The integrand $x\cos x$ is odd (odd × even) and the interval is symmetric, so the integral is 0; integration by parts confirms it.

steps.title: Symmetry
steps.body: $g(x) = x\cos x$ gives $g(-x) = (-x)\cos(-x) = -x\cos x = -g(x)$, so $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} g = 0$.

steps.title: By parts
steps.body: $\int x\cos x\,dx = x\sin x + \cos x$. So $[x\sin x + \cos x]_{-\pi}^{\pi} = (0 + (-1)) - (0 + (-1)) = 0$.

pitfalls: If the limits were $0$ to $\pi$ the value would be $(0-1) - (0+1) = -2$; the symmetric limits give 0.
cse-1998-b-60-b.verification: Symmetry argument and the antiderivative agree.

cse-1998-b-61.approach: Count the work per pivot column in forward elimination (a multiplier per lower row, then an update of the rest of that row and its right-hand side), sum over pivots, then add back substitution.

steps.title: Elimination, pivot $k$
steps.body: Rows $k+1..n$ ($n-k$ rows) each need 1 division for the multiplier $m = a_{ik}/a_{kk}$, then $(n-k)$ coefficients plus 1 right-hand side updated: $n-k+1$ multiply-adds. Pivot $k$ costs $(n-k)(n-k+1)$ multiply-adds and $n-k$ divisions.

steps.title: Sum over $k = 1..n-1$
steps.body:
With $j = n-k$:
$$\sum_{j=1}^{n-1} j(j+1) = \frac{(n-1)n(2n-1)}{6} + \frac{(n-1)n}{2} = \frac{(n-1)n(n+1)}{3} = \frac{n^3 - n}{3}$$
multiply-adds, and $\sum_{j=1}^{n-1} j = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ divisions.

steps.title: Back substitution
steps.body: $x_i = (b_i - \sum_{j>i} a_{ij}x_j)/a_{ii}$ needs $n-i$ multiply-adds and 1 division: $\sum_{i=1}^{n}(n-i) = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ multiply-adds and $n$ divisions.

steps.title: Total
steps.body:
Multiply-adds: $\frac{n^3-n}{3} + \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$. Counting divisions as operations too:
$$\frac{n^3-n}{3} + \frac{n(n-1)}{2} + \frac{n(n-1)}{2} + n = \frac{n^3}{3} + n^2 - \frac{n}{3}$$
which is $\approx n^3/3 = O(n^3)$.

answer.value: $\frac{n^3}{3} + n^2 - \frac{n}{3}$ operations: elimination $\frac{n^3-n}{3}$ multiply-adds + $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ divisions; back substitution $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ multiply-adds + $n$ divisions; $O(n^3)$

pitfalls: Forgetting the right-hand-side column in each row update (it adds the "+1" in $n-k+1$).
cse-1998-b-61.verification: $n = 2$: elimination 2 multiply-adds + 1 division, back substitution 1 multiply-add + 2 divisions = 6; formula $8/3 + 4 - 2/3 = 6$ ✓.

cse-1998-b-62-a.approach: Induct on $n \ge 3$; build an $(n+1)$-gon from an $n$-gon by inserting one new vertex on a side and count exactly which diagonals appear.

steps.title: Base case
steps.body: $n = 3$: a triangle has no diagonals, and $\frac{3(3-3)}{2} = 0$ ✓.

steps.title: Inductive step
steps.body:
Assume an $n$-gon has $\frac{n(n-3)}{2}$ diagonals. Insert a new vertex $v$ between adjacent vertices $u, w$. New diagonals:
- from $v$ to the $n - 2$ old vertices other than $u, w$;
- the old side $uw$, which is now a diagonal.
Old diagonals stay diagonals, so the count rises by $(n-2) + 1 = n - 1$.

steps.title: Algebra
steps.body:
$$\frac{n(n-3)}{2} + (n-1) = \frac{n^2 - 3n + 2n - 2}{2} = \frac{n^2 - n - 2}{2} = \frac{(n+1)(n-2)}{2} = \frac{(n+1)((n+1)-3)}{2}$$
which is the formula for $n+1$. $\blacksquare$

answer.value: Base $n=3$: $0$ diagonals. Step: a new vertex adds $(n-2)+1 = n-1$ diagonals, and $\frac{n(n-3)}{2} + n - 1 = \frac{(n+1)(n-2)}{2}$.

pitfalls: Forgetting that the old side $uw$ becomes a diagonal (gives $n-2$ instead of $n-1$).

cse-1998-b-62-b.approach: In a functional digraph made of disjoint cycles, $R^k$ moves each element $k$ steps along its cycle, so the powers repeat with period $\operatorname{lcm}$ of the cycle lengths.

steps.title: Read the digraph
steps.body: Component 1: $a \to b \to c \to a$ (length 3). Component 2: $d \to e \to f \to g \to h \to d$ (length 5). Each vertex has exactly one out-arc, so $R$ is a permutation.

steps.title: Powers
steps.body: $R^k$ sends $x$ to the vertex $k$ steps ahead. On the triangle $R^m = R^n \iff m \equiv n \pmod 3$; on the pentagon $\iff m \equiv n \pmod 5$. Both hold iff $15 \mid (n - m)$.

steps.title: Smallest pair
steps.body: With $m \ge 1$ the smallest choice is $m = 1$, $n = 1 + 15 = 16$: $R = R^{16}$. (If $R^0 = I_A$ were allowed, $R^0 = R^{15}$.)

pitfalls: Adding the cycle lengths ($3 + 5 = 8$) instead of taking their lcm.
cse-1998-b-62-b.verification: $R^{15}$ fixes every vertex (15 is a multiple of 3 and 5), so $R^{16} = R^{15}\circ R = R$; no smaller gap works since 15 is the least common multiple.

cse-1998-b-63-a.approach: An equivalence relation induced by a partition relates two elements exactly when they lie in the same block: take $B \times B$ for each block and union them.

steps.title: Block $\{d\}$ and union
steps.body: $\{d\}^2 = \{(d,d)\}$. Total $9 + 1 = 10$ ordered pairs.

cse-1998-b-63-b.approach: Draw one vertex per element and one arc per ordered pair from part (a): loops for $(x,x)$, two opposite arcs for each symmetric pair.

steps.title: Arcs from the 10 pairs
steps.body: Loops at $a, b, c, d$ (4 arcs). Opposite arcs $a \leftrightarrow b$, $a \leftrightarrow c$, $b \leftrightarrow c$ (6 arcs). Nothing joins $d$ to the others.

scene.caption: Six arcs inside the block {a, b, c}

steps.title: Shape
steps.body: The graph has two components, one per block: a complete symmetric cluster on $\{a,b,c\}$ with loops, and the single looped vertex $d$ — the picture of the partition $\Pi_1$.

scene.caption: One component per block of Π₁

answer.value: Loops at $a, b, c, d$; arcs both ways between each pair of $a, b, c$; $d$ joined to nothing else (10 arcs, two components $\{a,b,c\}$ and $\{d\}$).

animation.caption: Digraph of the equivalence relation induced by Π₁

cse-1998-b-63-b.verification: Arc count 10 matches the 10 ordered pairs of part (a).

cse-1998-b-63-c.approach: Partition $P$ refines $Q$ when every block of $P$ lies inside a block of $Q$. Check each pair; the finest partition is the bottom and the one-block partition is the top.

steps.title: Extremes
steps.body: $\Pi_2$ (all singletons) refines every partition; every partition refines $\Pi_3 = \{\{a,b,c,d\}\}$.

steps.title: $\Pi_1$ vs $\Pi_4$

animation.caption: Hasse diagram of the refinement order

cse-1998-b-64-a.approach: Use the contrapositive of the hypothesis — two elements that commute must be equal — and find two expressions that commute by associativity alone.

steps.title: Restate the hypothesis
steps.body: Hypothesis $(\ast)$: if $x * y = y * x$ then $x = y$ (contrapositive of the given condition).

steps.title: Find a commuting pair
steps.body: Take $x = a$, $y = a * a$. By associativity $a * (a * a) = (a * a) * a$, i.e. $x * y = y * x$.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: By $(\ast)$, $a = a * a$. $\blacksquare$

answer.value: $a*(a*a) = (a*a)*a$, so $a$ and $a*a$ commute and therefore $a*a = a$.

cse-1998-b-64-b.approach: Show $a*b*a$ commutes with $a$ using idempotence from (a); the hypothesis then forces $a*b*a = a$.

steps.title: Restate the hypothesis
steps.body: Hypothesis $(\ast)$: if $x * y = y * x$ then $x = y$ (contrapositive of the given condition).

steps.title: Commute with $a$
steps.body:
Let $x = a*b*a$. Using $a*a = a$:
$a * x = (a*a)*b*a = a*b*a = x$ and $x * a = a*b*(a*a) = a*b*a = x$. So $a*x = x*a$.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: By $(\ast)$, $x = a$, i.e. $a*b*a = a$. $\blacksquare$

answer.value: With $x = a*b*a$: $a*x = x = x*a$ (using $a*a=a$), so $x = a$.

cse-1998-b-64-b.verification: Both products reduce to $a*b*a$ in one use of (a).

cse-1998-b-64-c.approach: Show $y = a*b*c$ and $z = a*c$ commute; part (b) collapses the middle of each product. Then $(\ast)$ gives $y = z$.

steps.title: Restate the hypothesis
steps.body: Hypothesis $(\ast)$: if $x * y = y * x$ then $x = y$ (contrapositive of the given condition). Part (b) gives $x*y*x = x$ for all $x, y$.

steps.title: $y * z$
steps.body: $y*z = a*b*c*a*c = a*b*(c*a*c) = a*b*c$, since $c*a*c = c$ by (b).

steps.title: $z * y$
steps.body: $z*y = a*c*a*b*c = (a*c*a)*b*c = a*b*c$, since $a*c*a = a$ by (b).

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: $y*z = a*b*c = z*y$, so by $(\ast)$ $y = z$: $a*b*c = a*c$. $\blacksquare$

answer.value: $(a*b*c)*(a*c) = a*b*(c*a*c) = a*b*c$ and $(a*c)*(a*b*c) = (a*c*a)*b*c = a*b*c$, so they commute and $a*b*c = a*c$.

cse-1998-b-64-c.verification: Each product uses (b) once and associativity only.

cse-1998-b-65-a.approach: Trace which configurations can empty the stack. As printed, the 0-move needs $z_0$ on top and the 1-moves in $q_0$ never pop, so almost nothing is accepted; with the evidently intended rule $\delta(q_0,0,X)$ the PDA matches blocks $1^n0\,1^n0$.

steps.title: As printed
steps.body: From $(q_0, z_0)$: the $\epsilon$-move pops $z_0$ ⇒ $\epsilon$ accepted. Reading 0: $(q_1, X)$; then 1 pops $X$ ⇒ empty, so $01$ accepted. Reading 1 first pushes $X$; with $X$ on top $q_0$ has only $1$-moves that push, and the $\epsilon$-pop needs $z_0$, so the stack never empties. Hence $L = \{\epsilon, 01\}$.

steps.title: Intended fifth rule
steps.body: With $\delta(q_0, 0, X) = \{(q_1, X)\}$: in $q_0$ each 1 pushes an $X$ (n ≥ 1 needed so that $X$ is on top at the 0); the 0 moves to $q_1$; each 1 in $q_1$ pops an $X$; when $z_0$ reappears, a 0 returns to $(q_0, z_0)$, where the PDA can start a new block or pop $z_0$.

steps.title: Language
steps.body:
Each block is $1^n 0\,1^n 0$ with its own $n \ge 1$, repeated any number of times:
$$L = \{1^n 0\, 1^n 0 \mid n \ge 1\}^*$$
e.g. $\epsilon$, $1010$, $110110$, $1010110110$ are accepted; $10110$ is not.

answer.value: As printed: $\{\epsilon, 01\}$. With the intended rule $\delta(q_0,0,X)=\{(q_1,X)\}$: $L = \{1^n0\,1^n0 \mid n \ge 1\}^*$

pitfalls: Answering $0^n1^n$: no move pushes on 0, so 0s cannot be counted.
Forgetting $\epsilon$: the $\epsilon$-move pops $z_0$ immediately.

cse-1998-b-65-b.approach: Describe the role of each state and stack symbol: $q_0$ counts 1s, $q_1$ uncounts them, $z_0$ marks the block boundary.

steps.title: Counting phase ($q_0$)
steps.body: Each 1 pushes one $X$ ($\delta(q_0,1,z_0)$, $\delta(q_0,1,X)$), so after $1^n$ the stack is $X^n z_0$.

steps.title: Matching phase ($q_1$)
steps.body: The 0 switches to $q_1$ (intended rule $\delta(q_0,0,X)=\{(q_1,X)\}$); each 1 pops one $X$. A 0 is allowed only when $z_0$ is exposed, i.e. after exactly $n$ ones, and it returns to $q_0$ to start the next block.

steps.title: Acceptance
steps.body: In $q_0$ with $z_0$ on top the $\epsilon$-move pops $z_0$, emptying the store; so input is accepted iff it is a sequence of complete blocks $1^n0\,1^n0$. With the rule as printed only $\epsilon$ and $01$ empty the stack.

answer.value: $q_0$ pushes an $X$ per 1; the 0 moves to $q_1$, which pops an $X$ per 1; a 0 with $z_0$ exposed returns to $q_0$; popping $z_0$ by the $\epsilon$-move accepts — so it checks blocks $1^n0\,1^n0$ (as printed only $\epsilon$ and $01$).

cse-1998-b-66-a.approach: Read the grammar as nested pairs: $S_1$ wraps matching $a\ldots b$ around a core that has either extra $b$s ($B$) or extra $a$s ($A$).

steps.title: Helpers
steps.body: $B \to Bb \mid b$ gives $B = b^+$; $A \to aA \mid a$ gives $A = a^+$.

steps.title: Unfold $S_1$
steps.body:
Using $S_1 \to aS_1b$ $k \ge 0$ times: $S_1 \Rightarrow a^k\,(aBb \text{ or } aAb)\,b^k$.
- $aBb$: $a^{k+1} b^{p} b^{k+1}$, $p \ge 1$ ⇒ $a^i b^j$ with $j > i \ge 1$.
- $aAb$: $a^{k+1} a^{p} b^{k+1}$ ⇒ $a^i b^j$ with $i > j \ge 1$.

steps.title: Language
steps.body: $$L(G_1) = \{a^i b^j \mid i, j \ge 1,\ i \ne j\}$$

cse-1998-b-66-a.verification: $ab$ is not derivable (every core adds an extra letter); $aab$ and $abb$ are.

cse-1998-b-66-b.approach: Split $L_2$ by which halves are balanced: both, only the first, or only the second. $G_1$ supplies the unbalanced half; one new non-terminal $E$ supplies $a^nb^n$.

steps.title: Balanced block
steps.body: $E \to aEb \mid ab$ generates $\{a^nb^n \mid n \ge 1\}$ (2 rules).

steps.title: Cases
Grammar
steps.body:
$$S \to ES_1 \mid S_1E \mid EE,\qquad E \to aEb \mid ab$$
plus the productions of $G_1$ — exactly 5 new rules.

answer.value: $S \to ES_1 \mid S_1E \mid EE;\ E \to aEb \mid ab$ (with $G_1$)

pitfalls: Using $S \to EX \mid XE$ with $X$ for all $a^kb^l$ needs extra rules for $X$ and makes the grammar ambiguous.
cse-1998-b-66-b.verification: The three cases are exhaustive for "$i=j$ or $k=l$", and each is generated by its production.

cse-1998-b-66-c.approach: A language is inherently ambiguous only if every grammar for it is ambiguous; the grammar of (b) is unambiguous, so the answer is no.

steps.title: The halves split uniquely
steps.body: In $a^ib^ja^kb^l$ the only $b \to a$ boundary separates the two halves, so any derivation from $S$ must cut the string there.

steps.title: The three alternatives are disjoint
steps.body: $EE$: $i=j,\ k=l$; $ES_1$: $i=j,\ k\ne l$; $S_1E$: $i\ne j,\ k=l$. A string satisfies exactly one, so only one $S$-production applies.

steps.title: Parts are unambiguous
steps.body: $E \to aEb \mid ab$ has one derivation per $a^nb^n$. In $G_1$, $i > j$ forces $aAb$ with $k = j - 1$ wraps, $i < j$ forces $aBb$ with $k = i - 1$; $A$ and $B$ are linear. So every string of $L_2$ has one parse tree ⇒ $L_2$ is **not** inherently ambiguous.

answer.value: No — the grammar of part (b) is an unambiguous grammar for $L_2$.

pitfalls: Confusing $L_2$ with $\{a^ib^jc^k \mid i=j \text{ or } j=k\}$, which *is* inherently ambiguous because the two conditions share the $b$ block; here the conditions involve disjoint blocks.

cse-1998-b-67-a.approach: Feed the TTL pulse to a single input line the 8085 can sample in software — the SID pin (read with RIM) or one bit of an 8155/8255 port — and time it by counting a fixed-length polling loop (or gate an 8155/8253 timer with it).

steps.title: Minimum system
steps.body:
- **8085 CPU** with a crystal (e.g. 6 MHz → 3 MHz clock, $T = 0.333\,\mu s$).
- Address latch **74LS373** on $AD_0$–$AD_7$ driven by **ALE** to demultiplex the low address byte.
- **EPROM 2732/2764** for the program, **RAM 6116** (or an 8155, which gives 256 B RAM + ports + a 14-bit timer) for the count.
- Address decoder (**74LS138**) on $A_{15}$–$A_{11}$ produces the chip selects; $\overline{RD}$, $\overline{WR}$, $IO/\overline{M}$ give the read/write strobes.

steps.title: Connecting the pulse
steps.body:
The source is TTL compatible, so no level shifting is needed. Connect the pulse (through a 74LS14 Schmitt buffer for clean edges) to

- the **SID** pin (pin 5) — read by `RIM` into bit $D_7$ of A, **or**
- one input bit (say $PA_0$) of an **8155/8255** port configured as input.

Optionally connect it also to the **GATE** of an 8155/8253 counter so the hardware counts clock pulses only while the pulse is HIGH.

steps.title: Display / output
steps.body: The measured count (pulse width $= \text{count} \times \text{loop time}$) is stored in RAM or sent to an output port / seven-segment display driven by the second port of the 8155/8255.

answer.value: 8085 + latch + EPROM/RAM (or 8155) + decoder; TTL pulse wired to SID (read with RIM) or to an input bit of an 8155/8255 port (optionally to a timer GATE); width = loop count × loop time

cse-1998-b-67-a.shortcut: SID needs no extra chip: one wire plus RIM is the cheapest pulse input on the 8085.
pitfalls: Forgetting the address latch (ALE) needed to demultiplex AD0–AD7.
Starting the count in the middle of a pulse — the software must first wait for a rising edge.
cse-1998-b-67-a.verification: Checked that every block of the schematic (clock, demultiplexing, memory, decoding, input line) is required for the program in part (b) to run.

cse-1998-b-67-b.approach: Poll the input bit: wait for LOW (so we do not start inside a pulse), wait for the rising edge, then increment a 16-bit counter in a loop of known T-states until the line falls. Width = count × loop T-states × clock period.

steps.title: Assumptions
steps.body:
- Pulse on **SID**; `RIM` copies it into bit $D_7$ of A.
- 3 MHz clock ($T = 0.333\,\mu s$), no interrupts during measurement.
- Pulse shorter than $65535$ loop passes (16-bit counter in HL).
- Result stored at 2050H–2051H.

steps.title: Program
steps.body:
```asm
        LXI  H,0000H   ; HL = counter
WAITL:  RIM            ; A7 = SID
        ANI  80H
        JNZ  WAITL     ; wait while HIGH (skip a pulse already in progress)
WAITH:  RIM
        ANI  80H
        JZ   WAITH     ; wait for the rising edge
COUNT:  INX  H         ; 6 T
        RIM            ; 4 T
        ANI  80H       ; 7 T
        JNZ  COUNT     ; 10 T (taken) - loop while HIGH
        SHLD 2050H     ; save count
        HLT
```

steps.title: Converting the count
steps.body:
One pass of the `COUNT` loop takes $6+4+7+10 = 27$ T-states $= 27 \times 0.333\,\mu s = 9\,\mu s$.

$$\text{Width} \approx \text{count} \times 9\,\mu s$$

Resolution is $9\,\mu s$; the maximum measurable width is $65535 \times 9\,\mu s \approx 0.59\,s$.

answer.value: Wait for LOW, wait for rising edge, then loop {INX H; RIM; ANI 80H; JNZ} until the line goes LOW; width = count × 27 T-states (9 µs at 3 MHz)

pitfalls: INX H does not affect flags, so overflow of HL must be bounded by an assumption (or checked separately).
Using the T-states of the not-taken JNZ (7) for the loop — the loop repeats on the taken branch (10).
cse-1998-b-67-b.verification: 8085 T-states: INX rp = 6, RIM = 4, ANI = 7, JNZ taken = 10 → 27 per pass; 27 × 1/3 µs = 9 µs.

cse-1998-b-68.approach: Encode the states in binary (Q2Q1Q0), write the present-state/next-state table, treat the four unused states as don't-cares and read each D input directly from the table (D flip-flops: D = next state).

steps.title: Minimise each D
steps.body:
- $D_2 = 1$ only for 001; with don't-care 101: $D_2 = \overline{Q_1}\,Q_0$ (100 gives 0, 010/011 give 0).
- $D_1 = 1$ for 100 and 010, $0$ for 001 and 011: $D_1 = \overline{Q_0}$.
- $D_0 = 1$ for 010 and 011, $0$ for 001 and 100: $D_0 = Q_1$.

steps.title: Circuit
steps.body: Three D flip-flops on a common clock: $D_2 = \overline{Q_1}Q_0$ (one AND gate with $\overline{Q_1}$), $D_1 = \overline{Q_0}$, $D_0 = Q_1$. Initialise to 001 (preset $Q_0$).

steps.title: Self-starting check
steps.body: Unused states: $000 \to 010$, $101 \to 100$, $110 \to 011$, $111 \to 001$ — every one enters the main cycle $1\to4\to2\to3$ in one clock, so the counter is self-starting.

answer.value: D flip-flops (Q2Q1Q0): D2 = Q̄1·Q0, D1 = Q̄0, D0 = Q1 (001→100→010→011→001; self-starting)

pitfalls: Mixing the bit order of the state code between the table and the equations.
Not checking unused states — a counter can lock up in an unused loop.
cse-1998-b-68.verification: Applied the equations to each used state: 001 gives D2 = 1, D1 = 0, D0 = 0 → 100 ✓; 100 → 010 ✓; 010 → 011 ✓; 011 → 001 ✓.

cse-1998-b-69.approach: Work out which tracks/sides the 35 sectors occupy, then add initial rotational latency, the reading time (25 ms per sector at 300 RPM) and the track-to-track steps. The question leaves several assumptions open, so state them.
cse-1998-b-69.given:
| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Sectors / track | 8 |
| Sides | 2 |
| Speed | 300 RPM |
| Step time | 8 ms |
| Start | track 10, sector 3 (head already on track 10) |

steps.title: Rotation figures
steps.body: $300$ RPM $\Rightarrow$ one revolution $= 60/300 = 0.2\,s = 200$ ms; one sector $= 200/8 = 25$ ms.

steps.title: Where the 35 sectors are
steps.body: Sectors 3–8 of track 10, side 0: $6$; track 10, side 1: $8$ (total $14$); track 11, both sides: $16$ (total $30$); track 12, side 0: $5$ (total $35$). Switching sides is electronic (no seek), so only **2 steps** are needed ($10\to11$, $11\to12$).

steps.title: Add up (assumptions stated)
steps.body:
Assume: average initial latency of half a revolution $=100$ ms; the 1-sector buffer is emptied during the inter-sector gap, so consecutive sectors are read back-to-back; tracks are skewed so the first sector of the next track arrives just after the 8 ms step.

$$T = 100 + 35\times 25 + 2\times 8 = 100 + 875 + 16 = 991\text{ ms}$$

steps.title: Without track skew
steps.body:
If sector 1 of the new track is aligned with sector 1 of the old one, it has already passed when the 8 ms step completes, so each step costs a full revolution (200 ms):

$$T = 100 + 875 + 2\times 200 = 1375\text{ ms}$$

answer.value: ≈ 991 ms: 100 ms average initial rotational latency + 35 × 25 ms = 875 ms of reading + 2 track steps × 8 ms = 16 ms (sectors: 6 on track 10 side 0, 8 on track 10 side 1, 16 on track 11, 5 on track 12). If sector 1 of the next track is not skewed, each step costs a full revolution instead: 100 + 875 + 2 × 200 = 1375 ms.

pitfalls: Forgetting the second side: a cylinder (track 10) holds 16 sectors, not 8.
Answers of a few tens of ms are impossible — 35 sectors need at least 35 × 25 = 875 ms of reading alone.
cse-1998-b-69.verification: 6 + 8 + 16 + 5 = 35 sectors; lower bound 875 ms confirms the order of magnitude.

cse-1998-b-70.approach: Map the loop's n = km consecutive blocks onto the l sets (block i → set i mod l) and check whether every set can hold its share; if yes only the first pass misses. For l = 1 the loop exceeds the k-block cache and a cyclic access pattern defeats LRU/FIFO.

steps.title: Does the loop fit?
steps.body: Cache capacity $= l$ sets $\times k$ blocks $= kl$ blocks. Loop size $= n = km$ blocks with $m \le l$, so $km \le kl$. Consecutive blocks spread over the sets cyclically, so each set receives at most $\lceil km/l \rceil \le k$ blocks — every set can hold all of its loop blocks.

steps.title: Hit ratio for 1 < m ≤ l
steps.body:
Pass 1: each of the $n$ blocks misses once (compulsory). Passes 2–100: all hits.

$$h = \frac{100n - n}{100n} = \frac{99}{100} = 0.99$$

Counting individual word references ($b$ words per block): $h = 1 - \dfrac{n}{100\,n\,b} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{100b}$.

Average access time $t_{avg} = h\,t_c + (1-h)\,t_m$.

steps.title: Case l = 1
steps.body: One set of $k$ blocks (fully associative), but the loop has $mk > k$ blocks (since $m > 1$). With LRU (or FIFO) and a cyclic reference string longer than the cache, the block needed next is always the one just evicted, so **every block reference misses**: $h = 0$ (per word only the spatial-locality hits remain: $h = 1 - 1/b$).

answer.value: The loop (n = km blocks ≤ kl blocks) fits in the cache: only the first pass misses, so h = (100n − n)/(100n) = 0.99 per block reference (1 − 1/(100b) per word). For l = 1 the cache holds only k blocks but the loop has mk > k blocks, so with LRU/FIFO every block reference misses: h = 0 (1 − 1/b per word, from spatial locality only).

pitfalls: Assuming a set-associative cache can conflict even though each set receives at most k loop blocks.
Applying the 1 < m ≤ l formula to l = 1, where that range is empty and the loop no longer fits.
cse-1998-b-70.verification: Example: k = 2, l = 4, m = 3 → 6 blocks over 4 sets (2,2,1,1 per set ≤ 2) → 6 misses in 600 references → 0.99. With l = 1, k = 2, 4 blocks A B C D cycling under LRU: every access misses.

cse-1998-b-71-a.approach: Trace the four assignments on a concrete list p → X → Y → Z.

steps.title: Name the nodes
steps.body: Let p point to node P with $P \to X \to Y \to Z$.

steps.title: Trace
steps.body:
1. `q := p->next` → $q = X$.
2. `p->next := q->next` → $P \to Y$.
3. `q->next := (q->next)->next` → $X$'s next was $Y$, so $X \to Z$.
4. `(p->next)->next := q` → $Y \to X$.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: List is now $P \to Y \to X \to Z$: the **two nodes following p are swapped** (by relinking, not by copying data).

answer.value: Swaps the two nodes that follow p (p→X→Y→Z becomes p→Y→X→Z)

pitfalls: Step 3 uses q->next before it is overwritten — it reads the old link X → Y.
cse-1998-b-71-a.verification: Walk from P after the trace: P → Y → X → Z, every node reached exactly once, no cycle.

cse-1998-b-71-b.approach: Use precedence: function application binds tightest, then * and /, then −; left-to-right for equal precedence.

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: Postfix: `3 x 1 + log * a 2 / -`

pitfalls: Placing log before its argument (prefix style) — in postfix the unary operator follows its operand.
cse-1998-b-71-b.verification: Evaluating the postfix with a stack: push 3, x, 1; + → x+1; log → log(x+1); * → 3·log(x+1); push a, 2; / → a/2; − → original expression.

cse-1998-b-72.approach: Last postorder element is the root; split the inorder sequence around it and recurse on each side with the matching postorder segment.

steps.title: Root
steps.body: Postorder ends with **b** → root $= b$. Inorder `a f | b | c d g e`: left $\{a,f\}$, right $\{c,d,g,e\}$. Postorder splits the same way: `a f | c g e d | b`.

steps.title: Left subtree
steps.body: Postorder `a f` → root **f**; inorder `a f` → a is f's left child.

steps.title: Right subtree
steps.body: Postorder `c g e d` → root **d**; inorder `c | d | g e` → left child c, right part $\{g,e\}$ with postorder `g e` → root **e**, inorder `g e` → g is e's left child.

answer.value: Root b; left subtree f with left child a; right subtree d with left child c and right child e, where e has left child g

pitfalls: Using the first postorder element as root (that is preorder's rule).
cse-1998-b-72.verification: Inorder of the built tree: a f b c d g e ✓; postorder: a f c g e d b ✓.

cse-1998-b-73-a.approach: The sparsest AVL tree of height h has one subtree of height h−1 and the other of height h−2 (the most unbalanced allowed), each itself minimal.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Root + minimal AVL tree of height $h-1$ + minimal AVL tree of height $h-2$ (heights may differ by at most 1).

steps.title: Recurrence
steps.body:
Height = edges on the longest root–leaf path (single node has height 0):

$$N(h) = N(h-1) + N(h-2) + 1,\quad N(0) = 1,\ N(1) = 2$$

This gives $N(h) = F_{h+3} - 1$ (Fibonacci).

pitfalls: If height counts levels (single node = height 1) the base cases shift to N(1) = 1, N(2) = 2.
cse-1998-b-73-a.verification: N(2) = 2 + 1 + 1 = 4: root, a 2-node child and a leaf — the smallest AVL tree of height 2.

cse-1998-b-73-b.approach: Unroll N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1 from N(0) = 1, N(1) = 2.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Smallest AVL tree of height 8 has **88** nodes (height in edges). With height counted in levels it would be $N(8) = 54$.

pitfalls: Mixing the two height conventions — check N(0)/N(1) before iterating.

cse-1998-b-74-a.approach: One mandatory letter followed by 0 to 5 letters or digits.

steps.title: Build
steps.body: Let $L = (a+b+\dots+z+A+\dots+Z)$, $D = (0+1+\dots+9)$. First character: $L$. Remaining $0$–$5$ characters, each $L$ or $D$: $(L+D+\epsilon)^5$.

steps.title: Expression
steps.body: $$L\,(L+D+\epsilon)^5 \;=\; L\big(\epsilon + (L+D) + (L+D)^2 + \dots + (L+D)^5\big)$$

pitfalls: Writing L(L+D)* — that allows identifiers longer than six characters.
cse-1998-b-74-a.verification: Lengths produced: 1 (all ε) up to 6 (no ε) — exactly "up to six", first symbol always a letter.

cse-1998-b-74-b.approach: Compute FIRST of each right-hand side and FOLLOW for the ε-producing Y; place A → α under FIRST(α), and Y → ε under FOLLOW(Y).

| Non-terminal | FIRST | FOLLOW |

| Program | begin | \$ |
| X | d, s | end |

| X | | X → d semi X | X → sY | | |
| Y | | | | Y → semi s Y | Y → ε |

No cell has two entries, confirming the grammar is LL(1).

cse-1998-b-75.approach: Synthesise for each L both its integer value and its length; the fractional part is L2.val / 2^{L2.len}.

steps.title: Attributes
steps.body: `L.val` (value of the bit string as an integer), `L.len` (number of bits), `B.val`, `S.val` — all synthesized.

steps.title: Translation scheme
steps.body:
| Production | Semantic rule |
|---|---|
| $S \to L_1 . L_2$ | $S.val = L_1.val + L_2.val / 2^{L_2.len}$ |
| $S \to L$ | $S.val = L.val$ |
| $L \to L_1 B$ | $L.val = 2 L_1.val + B.val$; $L.len = L_1.len + 1$ |
| $L \to B$ | $L.val = B.val$; $L.len = 1$ |
| $B \to 0$ | $B.val = 0$ |
| $B \to 1$ | $B.val = 1$ |

cse-1998-b-76-a.approach: Average response (turnaround) time is minimised by Shortest Job First; place x according to its size.

steps.title: Why SJF
steps.body: With jobs run back-to-back, the $i$-th job's completion adds its run time to every later job, so the total is $\sum (n-i+1)\,t_i$; it is minimised by running the shortest job first (exchange argument).

pitfalls: Giving one fixed order — the position of x depends on its value.
cse-1998-b-76-a.verification: Swapping any adjacent pair with the longer job first increases the total by (longer − shorter) > 0.

cse-1998-b-76-b.approach: Read the graph: after S1, two independent branches run concurrently — S3 alone and the chain S2 → S4 — and S5 waits for both. The direct edges S1→S4 and S1→S5 are implied by the others.

steps.title: Dependencies
steps.body: Edges: $S_1\to S_2, S_1\to S_3, S_1\to S_4, S_1\to S_5, S_2\to S_4, S_3\to S_5, S_4\to S_5$. $S_1\to S_4$ follows from $S_1\to S_2\to S_4$ and $S_1\to S_5$ from $S_1\to S_3\to S_5$, so they need no extra code.

steps.title: Program

answer.value: S1; parbegin S3; begin S2; S4 end parend; S5

pitfalls: Putting S2, S3 and S4 all in one parbegin — S4 must wait for S2.
cse-1998-b-76-b.verification: Every edge is respected: S1 precedes the parbegin, S2 precedes S4 inside the sequential block, and S5 starts only after parend (both S3 and S4 done).

cse-1998-b-77-a.approach: Compare the sizes: a free list stores one D-bit address per free block; a bit map stores one bit per block.

steps.title: Sizes
steps.body: Free list: $F \cdot D$ bits. Bit map: one bit per block $= 13$ bits (in general $B$ bits for $B$ blocks).

steps.title: Condition
steps.body: Free list is smaller when $F\cdot D < 13$ (generally $F \cdot D < B$, i.e. $F/B < 1/D$).

answer.value: F·D < 13 (in general F·D < B for B blocks)

pitfalls: Comparing with the number of free blocks instead of the total number of blocks for the bit map.
cse-1998-b-77-a.verification: With D = 16 and B = 13 the free list wins only when F = 0 — consistent with bit maps being preferred on small disks.

cse-1998-b-77-b.approach: Since a record is exactly one sector, convert the start address to a linear sector number, add n, and convert back with division and remainders.

steps.title: Linearise the start
steps.body: Number cylinders, tracks and sectors from 0. Sectors per cylinder $= t\cdot s$. Start: $N_0 = (c_L\, t + t_L)\, s + s_L$.

steps.title: Record n
steps.body: With $r_l = s_l$, record $n$ (first record $n=0$) occupies sector $N = N_0 + n$.

steps.title: Back to CHS
steps.body:
$$\text{cylinder} = \left\lfloor \frac{N}{t\,s} \right\rfloor,\quad \text{track} = \left\lfloor \frac{N \bmod (t\,s)}{s} \right\rfloor,\quad \text{sector} = N \bmod s$$

(If records are numbered from 1, use $n-1$; if sectors are numbered from 1, add 1 to the sector.)

answer.value: With N = (c_L·t + t_L)·s + s_L + n (records numbered from 0): cylinder = ⌊N/(t·s)⌋, track = ⌊(N mod t·s)/s⌋, sector = N mod s

pitfalls: Forgetting that a contiguous file wraps from the last sector of a track to the next track and then the next cylinder.
cse-1998-b-77-b.verification: t = 2, s = 4, start (0,1,3), n = 1: N = (0+1)·4 + 3 + 1 = 8 → cylinder 1, track 0, sector 0 — the sector right after (0,1,3) ✓.

cse-1998-b-78-a.approach: List the FDs implied by the meaning, then test 2NF (partial dependency) and 3NF (transitive dependency).

steps.title: FDs
steps.body: Book-id → Subject-Category, Name-of-Author; Name-of-Author → Nationality-of-Author.

steps.title: Test
steps.body: Key is the single attribute Book-id, so no partial dependency → **2NF**. But Book-id → Name-of-Author → Nationality-of-Author is transitive (Nationality is non-prime and Author is not a superkey) → not 3NF.

pitfalls: Calling it 3NF because the key is a single attribute — that only guarantees 2NF.
cse-1998-b-78-a.verification: Decomposing into (Book-id, Subject, Author) and (Author, Nationality) removes the transitive dependency, confirming 3NF was violated.

cse-1998-b-78-b.approach: With the composite key (Name-of-Author, Book-title), attributes depending on Name-of-Author alone are partial dependencies.

steps.title: FDs
steps.body: Name-of-Author → Nationality-of-Author, Author-address (author facts); (Name-of-Author, Book-title) → Book-id, Subject-Category.

steps.title: Test
steps.body: Nationality and Author-address are non-prime and depend on **part** of the key (Name-of-Author) → partial dependency → not 2NF. Attributes are atomic → **1NF**.

pitfalls: Overlooking that Name-of-Author is only part of the new key.
cse-1998-b-78-b.verification: Any non-prime attribute determined by a proper subset of a candidate key violates 2NF — Nationality is such an attribute.

cse-1998-b-79.approach: Find courses having at least one prerequisite the student has NOT completed, and subtract them from all courses (division via set difference).

steps.title: Courses done by 2310
steps.body: $T \leftarrow \rho_{T(\text{pre-Cno})}\big(\pi_{Cno}(\sigma_{\text{student no}=2310}(\text{COMPLETED}))\big)$

steps.title: Missing prerequisites
steps.body: $\text{PRE-REQ} - (\pi_{Cno}(\text{PRE-REQ}) \times T)$ keeps exactly the pairs (Cno, pre-Cno) whose pre-Cno is not in $T$.

steps.title: Result
steps.body:
$$\pi_{Cno}(\text{COURSES}) - \pi_{Cno}\big(\text{PRE-REQ} - (\pi_{Cno}(\text{PRE-REQ}) \times T)\big)$$

Courses with no prerequisites are included (vacuously all completed).

answer.value: T ← ρ_{pre-Cno}(π_Cno(σ_{student no=2310}(COMPLETED))); result = π_Cno(COURSES) − π_Cno(PRE-REQ − (π_Cno(PRE-REQ) × T))

cse-1998-b-79.shortcut: Equivalently π_Cno(COURSES) − π_Cno(PRE-REQ ▷ T) (anti-join on pre-Cno).
pitfalls: Using PRE-REQ ÷ T — that returns courses whose prerequisites include ALL of the student's completed courses, the reverse condition.
cse-1998-b-79.verification: Example: PRE-REQ = {(C3,C1),(C3,C2),(C4,C1)}, T = {C1}: missing pairs = {(C3,C2)} → result = all courses except C3 ✓.
